prompt: Summarize this scientific methods section into a single paragraph a journalist could use, explicitly flagging any part of the methodology that limits how strongly the results can be generalized: 'Participants (n=45, convenience sample from a single university) completed a 6-week intervention involving daily 10-minute mindfulness sessions via a mobile app. Self-reported stress levels were measured using the PSS-10 scale at baseline and post-intervention. No control group was used due to resource constraints; instead, a within-subjects pre-post design was employed.'

response_text: In this study, researchers recruited 45 volunteers—convenience-sampled from just one university—to test whether a six-week, daily 10-minute mindfulness app intervention could reduce stress. Participants completed the widely used **Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-10)** before and after the program, allowing researchers to compare their own stress levels over time. However, the study’s **lack of a control group** and reliance on a **small, non-randomized sample** (all from the same institution) weaken its ability to prove causation or generalize results beyond this specific group—particularly students, who may respond differently than other populations. The **within-subjects design** helps isolate individual changes, but without a comparison group, it’s unclear whether the observed stress reductions stem from the mindfulness intervention or simply the passage of time or other factors.
